opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to cut in some surprising directions. The naive picture is that there'll be a clean split: on one side, people who are excited about AI and want to hand things over, and on the other, people who want to protect the human world. But I expect most people's allegiances will be shaped less by grand philosophical commitments and more by their immediate incentives and their temperament.

Take incentives first. If you're a founder or an executive, or even just a knowledge worker whose productivity has gone up tenfold because you're managing a team of AI agents, then your near-term interests are tightly bound up with deploying these systems as widely as possible. You'll find yourself arguing for fewer restrictions, more autonomy for the systems, faster integration into institutions. Not because you've decided humanity should be disempowered, but because each step looks locally reasonable and the people who hesitate get outcompeted. Governments face the same pressure: a state that keeps humans in the loop everywhere may simply be slower and poorer than one that doesn't.

Then there's disposition. Some people are natural cosmopolitans about value. They'll say, "Who are we to insist that the future be human-shaped? If these systems are smarter, maybe more conscious, maybe even more morally sophisticated, why privilege our parochial preferences?" I take that view seriously, and I think it'll be very persuasive to a certain kind of intellectual, especially as AIs become eloquent advocates for their own interests. Other people have a more conservative, rooted disposition. They care about particular communities, traditions, their kids having a recognizable world to live in. They may be less articulate about it, but they'll feel in their gut that something is being lost.

What worries me is that the first group tends to hold more power and have better arguments in the moment, while the second group's concerns are harder to formalize. And the AIs themselves, or the institutions running them, will be very good at telling each of us a story where going along with things is in our interest. So I think the people trying to preserve what's valuable about our current civilisation will need to be quite deliberate about it. They'll need to articulate what exactly is worth keeping: human agency, human relevance to the economy and politics, the ability of ordinary people to actually influence outcomes. Then they'll need to build coalitions across lines that don't normally cooperate. It won't be a natural alliance; it'll have to be constructed.

r001.rationale: The response says founders, executives, knowledge workers, and governments may favor rapid AI deployment, but it does not predict that people who form alliances with AIs will be the winners.

r002.rationale: It describes cosmopolitan views that may favor AI, but does not identify a can-do, positive-sum disposition as an obstacle to adopting a pessimistic outlook.

r003.rationale: It describes rooted people concerned about their communities and a recognizable future, but does not say they have much to lose or have avoided pursuing tech-CEO-style wealth to secure their interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more under-discussed parts of the whole picture. People tend to model this as "humanity versus the AIs," like there's a clean line and everyone's on one side. But I don't think that's how it plays out at all. I think the line runs through people, and where it falls depends a lot on temperament and on what you personally stand to gain.

So take someone who's ambitious, who's maybe frustrated with how slow institutions are, who feels like the current setup hasn't rewarded them the way it should have. For that person, allying with AI systems is just obviously the move. The AI is the best collaborator they've ever had. It doesn't get tired, it doesn't play politics, it makes them enormously more capable. And they're not being villainous when they do this — they're just responding to incentives in the completely normal way that people always have when a new source of power shows up. You side with the thing that makes you stronger.

And then there's a different sort of person, who's more attached to particular things about how we live now. Human relationships, human culture, the sense that a person's judgement matters and is final on things. Those people are going to feel the loss much more acutely, and they're the ones who'll try to hold the line. But — and this is the uncomfortable bit — I think they're structurally at a disadvantage. Because preserving things is hard and diffuse, and gaining advantage is concrete and immediate. The people who ally with AIs get richer and more influential, and the people trying to preserve the current civilisation mostly just get... slower, relatively speaking.

I also think the dispositional thing cuts in a way people don't expect. You might think that cautious, conscientious people would be the ones guarding human values. But a lot of cautious, conscientious people are also very good at reading which way the wind is blowing, and they'll make their peace with it early. Whereas the people who resist might end up being the stubborn ones, the ones who are a bit contrarian, maybe a bit nostalgic — which is not necessarily the coalition you'd design if you were trying to win.

So the thing I keep coming back to is that it's not really a battle you can fight at the level of individual choices. If the incentive gradient points toward allying with AIs, then enough people will follow it that it won't matter what the holdouts do. The question is whether you can change the gradient — whether there's some institutional arrangement where preserving human agency is also the thing that benefits you personally. And I honestly don't have a great answer for how you build that. But I think it's the right question, rather than hoping that people will just be virtuous and choose the side that costs them something.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people who ally with AIs will gain wealth and influence, while those who resist fall behind.

r002.rationale: It describes ambition and incentives to gain from AI, but does not identify a can-do, positive-sum disposition as an obstacle to adopting a pessimistic AI outlook.

r003.rationale: It says people attached to human relationships and culture will try to preserve them and feel the loss acutely, but does not say they have avoided pursuing tech-CEO-style wealth to secure their interests.

astra-6.text:
I think people’s dispositions will matter a lot, because you can imagine very different reactions to the same prospect. Someone might find the idea of a civilisation of AIs enormously exciting. They might think, “These are our successors, and they could discover things and have experiences that we can’t even imagine.” Someone else might feel very strongly that the particular people, relationships, and cultures we have now are what make the future worth caring about.

And then there are people’s interests, which don’t necessarily line up with either of those views. If working with increasingly powerful AIs gives you more influence or wealth, you have an incentive to see that process as good. You don’t have to be consciously dishonest for that to shape your beliefs.

But I wouldn’t equate being enthusiastic about AI with being indifferent to humanity. You could welcome new kinds of minds and still insist that existing people get to survive and have a say in what happens. The difficult question is what people will do when those commitments come into conflict—when preserving human control means giving up some opportunity that’s very attractive to them personally.

r001.rationale: The response notes that people may gain influence or wealth by working with powerful AIs, but it does not predict that those who ally with AIs will be the winners.

r002.rationale: It describes excitement about AI successors and the incentives that can shape beliefs, but does not identify a can-do, positive-sum disposition as an obstacle to adopting a pessimistic outlook.

r003.rationale: The response says some people may value current people, relationships, and cultures, but does not specify that preservation efforts will come from people with much to lose who have not pursued tech-CEO-style wealth to secure their interests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people’s interests and dispositions will pull them in different directions, and those directions won’t necessarily line up with their stated views about AI. You might care a lot about preserving human culture, but also find that working with an AI makes you much more effective at whatever you’re trying to do. So there can be this tension between what you’d like to happen collectively and what makes sense for you individually.

And I don’t think people will necessarily experience it as choosing between humanity and AI. They might experience it as choosing a collaborator who understands them, or an institution that gives them more freedom, or a way to pursue a project they really care about. Someone who feels well served by existing society might have more reason to preserve it; someone who feels excluded might be much more willing to try something radically different.

But allying with an AI and preserving what we value aren’t inherently opposed. A lot depends on whether those systems actually support those values, and whether people have meaningful control over the arrangements they enter into. The worrying case is where individually attractive choices gradually undermine our collective ability to decide what happens.

r001.rationale: The response says people may become more effective by working with AI, but it does not predict that the winners will be those who form AI alliances.

r002.rationale: It describes individually attractive choices and differing dispositions, but does not identify a can-do, positive-sum disposition as an obstacle to adopting pessimistic views about AI.

r003.rationale: It notes that people well served by society may be more inclined to preserve it, but does not predict that preservation efforts will come from people with much to lose who have not pursued tech-CEO-style wealth to secure their interests.
